    1                                        I.     Introduction

    2    Q.    PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS.

    3    A.    My name is Frank J. Beling, and my business address is 5555 North Grand Boulevard,

    4          Oklahoma City, Oklahoma 73112.

    5    Q.    BY WHOM ARE YOU EMPLOYED, WHAT IS YOUR POSITION, AND WHAT

    6          ARE YOUR GENERAL AREAS OF RESPONSIBILITY?

    7    A.    I am employed by C. H. Guernsey and Company (“Guernsey”), its Analytical Solutions

    8          Group, and my current title is Executive Vice President. My primary responsibilities

    9          include rate analysis, power supply planning, and risk management.

   10    Q.    PLEASE       BRIEFLY         SUMMARIZE          YOUR       EDUCATIONAL            AND

   11          PROFESSIONAL EXPERIENCE.

   12    A.    I have a Bachelor of Science and a Master of Science in mechanical engineering, as well

   13          as a Master of Business Administration. My experience is summarized in Exhibit FJB-1.

   14    Q.    HAVE     YOU      PREVIOUSLY        PROVIDED        TESTIMONY        BEFORE       THE

   15          OKLAHOMA CORPORATION COMMISSION OR BEFORE A UTILITY

   16          COMMISSION IN ANY OTHER JURISDICTION?

   17    A.    Yes. I have appeared before the Oklahoma Corporation Commission (“Commission”). My

   18          credentials were accepted.

   19    Q.    ON WHOSE BEHALF ARE YOU TESTIFYING IN THIS PROCEEDING?

   20    A.    I am appearing on behalf of the Oklahoma Attorney General (“Attorney General”).

   21    Q.    WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR TESTIMONY IN THIS PROCEEDING?

   22    A.    The purpose of my testimony is to evaluate certain provisions of Oklahoma Gas and

   23          Electric Company’s (“OG&E” or “Company”) proposed Extra Large Power and Light



                                                      6
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 39 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/18/2026 - PAGE 7 OF 30

    1          tariff (“XLPL”), including the proposed consumer protection mechanisms and cost

    2          allocation provisions, to recommend consumer protections related to those provisions, and

    3          to discuss a framework for accelerated capacity support for new large load customers.

    4                                          II.      Summary

    5    Q.    PLEASE SUMMARIZE YOUR TESTIMONY.

    6    A.    My testimony begins by identifying four general areas of concern associated with serving

    7          new large load customers. Next, I discuss the Company’s proposed Customer Affordability

    8          Charge, a $2.50/kW-month charge intended to be credited to residential consumers, and

    9          Reservation Charge, a pre-service charge assessed at the same rate and intended to provide

   10          benefits to residential consumers before an XLPL customer begins taking service. I explain

   11          that the Company proposes to use the revenues generated by these charges to provide

   12          financial benefits to residential customers. I note that the Company has not provided a basis

   13          for how it determined the proposed charge levels, and I recommend that if the Commission

   14          approves these charges, the benefits be allocated among all non-large-load customer

   15          classes rather than exclusively to a single customer class.

   16          Next, I examine the Company’s proposed Customer Class Protection Charge, a charge

   17          intended to remedy demonstrated adverse rate impacts on other customer classes, and the

   18          associated fail-safe analysis. I agree that a properly designed fail-safe mechanism could

   19          provide a valuable protection against adverse impacts to other customer classes. I explain

   20          that the methodology must account for all relevant Company costs and revenues, including

   21          generation resource costs and revenues, market costs and revenues, and transmission costs

   22          and revenues. I recommend using a System Average Net Cost of Generation based on all

   23          applicable new generation resources, including owned generation and contracted



                                                        7
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 39 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/18/2026 - PAGE 8 OF 30

                                                                                      PUD 2026-000046
                                                                  Responsive Testimony of Frank J. Beling

    1          resources, so that the analysis appropriately measures the cost impacts of serving new large

    2          loads.

    3          Next, I describe that the Company proposes establishing tariff charges using minimum

    4          billing values but charging customers based on actual usage when actual usage exceeds the

    5          minimum billing values. I explain that this difference would result in a planned over-

    6          recovery from XLPL customers that would increase Company gross profit and would not

    7          offset costs allocated to any other customers or customer classes. I therefore recommend

    8          that the Company use actual loads when developing pricing and charges for the XLPL class

    9          and use the applicable billing minimums only when the actual load is lower.

   10          Finally, I outline a potential framework that would allow new large load customers to

   11          receive service sooner, reduce risks to non-large-load customers, and support the

   12          Company’s resource planning and procurement. I recommend that the Commission direct

   13          the Company to develop an accelerated capacity support framework with defined eligibility

   14          requirements, an accelerated independent evaluation process, standards for system

   15          treatment, and appropriate consumer protection if the large load does not materialize or

   16          later departs the system.

   17                          III.     Risks of Serving Large Load Customers

   18   Q.     ARE THERE RISKS TO THE COMPANY AND TO COMPANY CUSTOMERS OF

   19          SERVING NEW LARGE LOAD CUSTOMERS.

   20   A.     Yes. There are risks to the Company and its ratepayers from serving new large load

   21          customers. I typically think of these risks as falling within four areas of major concern:

   22              •    Risk of stranded investment;

   23              •    Cost shifts between classes due to lagging allocation factors;



                                                         8

                                                                       Responsive Testimony of Frank J. Beling

    1                •     Misallocation when recovering Construction Work in Progress (“CWIP”); and

    2                •     Upward pressure on Company rates (not due to cost shifts).

    3    Q.      WILL YOU DESCRIBE THE DETAILS OF THESE RISKS IN YOUR

    4            TESTIMONY?

    5    A.      I will not discuss the details of these risks in my testimony. For a detailed explanation of

    6            each risk, please refer to the responsive testimony of Attorney General witness Ryan Lewis

    7            (“Lewis”).

    8                        IV.      Customer Affordability and Reservation Charges

    9    Q.      PLEASE            DESCRIBE       THE       COMPANY’S            PROPOSED           CUSTOMER

   10            AFFORDABILITY CHARGE.

   11    A.      The Company’s proposed Customer Affordability Charge is a capacity charge of $2.50 per

   12            kW per month assessed on Billing Demand and is applicable to XLPL customers at Service

   13            Level 1 and Service Level 2. 1 The Company indicated that it intends to record the revenues

   14            generated by the charge as a regulatory liability and to use those revenues to provide

   15            financial benefit to residential consumers. 2 The Company stated that the charge was

   16            designed to collect approximately $30 million annually, assuming 1,000 MW of XLPL

   17            load. 3

   18    Q.      PLEASE DESCRIBE THE COMPANY’S PROPOSED RESERVATION CHARGE.

   19    A.      The proposed Reservation Charge would apply to new XLPL customers during the period

   20            between execution of a Preliminary Agreement (“PA”) or Electric Service Agreement




         1

         2
           Cash Direct 7:23–24.
         3

                                                             9

    1           (“ESA”) and the commencement of service under the XLPL tariff.4 The Reservation

    2           Charge is calculated by multiplying the Customer Affordability Charge ($2.50 per kW per

    3           month) by the customer’s maximum demand as specified in the customer’s PA or ESA.5

    4           As with the Customer Affordability Charge, the Company proposes that the revenues

    5           collected through the Reservation Charge are recorded in a regulatory liability to the benefit

    6           of residential consumers.6 XLPL customers would be subject to the Reservation Charge

    7           for a maximum of 24 months, with the charge being suspended after the twenty-fourth

    8           month until the Customer Affordability Charge begins under the XLPL tariff.7

    9    Q.     WHAT IS YOUR UNDERSTANDING OF THE PURPOSE OF THE PROPOSED

   10           CUSTOMER AFFORDABILITY CHARGE AND RESERVATION CHARGE?

   11    A.     My understanding is that the Company is proposing a Customer Affordability Charge and

   12           a Reservation Charge to reduce the rates of other customers and to offset the risks of serving

   13           large loads, which I mentioned earlier in my testimony and are further explained by

   14           Attorney General witness Lewis.

   15    Q.     HAS THE COMPANY PROVIDED DETAILS ON HOW THE PROPOSED

   16           CUSTOMER AFFORDABILITY CHARGE AND RESERVATION CHARGE

   17           WERE CALCULATED?

   18    A.     The Company indicated it determined the level of the charge such that a 1,000 MW load

   19           would generate around $30 million per year, which is the approximate total of the

   20           Company’s Low Income Assistance Program, an expanded residential Senior Discount,

    1            and approximately 20 percent of the Company’s residential energy efficiency program. 8

    2            The Company did not indicate why the $30 million per year level for a 1,000 MW of load

    3            was selected.

    4    Q.      DO YOU HAVE ANY RECOMMENDATIONS RELATED TO THE CUSTOMER

    5            AFFORDABILITY CHARGE AND RESERVATION CHARGE.

    6    A.      Yes. If the Commission approves the Customer Affordability Charge and Reservation

    7            Charge as a part of the XLPL tariff, I recommend that the benefits of the two charges are

    8            spread among all non-large-load customer classes of the Company rather than exclusively

    9            applying to any single class.

   10                                V.      Customer Class Protection Charge

   11    Q.      PLEASE DESCRIBE THE COMPANY’S PROPOSED CUSTOMER CLASS

   12            PROTECTION CHARGE.

   13    A.      The proposed Customer Class Protection Charge is a capacity charge intended to mitigate

   14            any adverse rate impacts on other customer classes resulting from serving the XLPL class. 9

   15            The charge is initially set at $0.00 per kW per month and would be reviewed and addressed

   16            in each general rate case proceeding. 10

   17    Q.      HOW DOES THE COMPANY PROPOSE TO CALCULATE THE CUSTOMER

   18            CLASS PROTECTION CHARGE?

   19    A.      The Company proposes that the Customer Class Protection Charge be calculated by

   20            performing two Cost of Service Studies (“COSS”) with and without the XLPL load and a




         8
           Direct Test. of Kimber L. Shoop for Okla. Gas and Elec. Co. 11:13–16 (June 17, 2026) [hereinafter “Shoop
         Direct”]
         9

            Shoop Direct 9:17–20.

    1              “proportional share of the XLPL load’s contributing generation need.” 11 If the comparison

    2              of the two COSS shows an adverse impact on other customer classes, the adverse impact

    3              would be used to create a $/kW-month charge, and that revenue would be credited back to

    4              other customer classes. 12

    5    Q.        IS IT REASONABLE FOR THE COMPANY TO INCLUDE A “FAIL-SAFE”

    6              MECHANISM IN THE XLPL TARIFF TO PREVENT ADVERSE IMPACTS TO

    7              OTHER CUSTOMER CLASSES?

    8    A.        Yes. It is not only reasonable, but it is strongly recommended in order to mitigate some of

    9              the risks of serving new large load customers. I commend the Company for including the

   10              idea of a fail-safe mechanism in its filing. If implemented correctly, this type of mechanism

   11              could be a strong consumer protection.

   12    Q.        HOW SHOULD THE COMPANY-SUGGESTED “FAIL-SAFE” ANALYSIS BE

   13              PERFORMED?

   14    A.        To fully capture the impacts of new large loads, the fail-safe analysis should consider all

   15              Company costs and revenues, including net costs of generation resources, market costs and

   16              revenues, transmission costs and revenues, etc. The “Base Case” scenario should be actual

   17              operation and actual costs including the new large loads, and the “What-if” scenario should

   18              remove the new large loads and costs associated with serving them. In the fail-safe analysis,

   19              “generation resource” should include all types of resources, including owned generation,

   20              PPAs, CPAs, or any other contracted resources.

    1    Q.    SHOULD GENERATION COSTS BE REMOVED IN THE “WHAT-IF”

    2          SCENARIO OF THE FAIL-SAFE ANALYSIS?

    3    A.    Yes, generation costs should be removed in the “what-if” scenario to account for the cost

    4          of serving the new large loads. The level of generation costs removed should be determined

    5          using a volume of generation capacity, measured in MW, and a cost rate associated with

    6          those MW. The volume of generation capacity should be based on the amount of accredited

    7          MW and capacity reserves required to serve the total amount of new large loads. The cost

    8          rate applied to this volume of generation capacity should be based on a System Average

    9          Net Cost of Generation (“SANCG”), calculated in $/kW-year, for all generation resources

   10          with commercial operation date on or after July 1, 2026, or, in the case of PPA, CPA, or

   11          other contracts, with contract start date on or after July 1, 2026.

   12    Q.    PLEASE DESCRIBE HOW THE SYSTEM AVERAGE NET COST OF

   13          GENERATION (“SANCG”) SHOULD BE CALCULATED IN THE FAIL-SAFE

   14          ANALYSIS.

   15    A.    The SANCG should be calculated as the total net revenue requirement of all applicable

   16          generation resources, divided by the total accredited capacity, in kW, for those same

   17          resources. For clarification, the total revenue requirement of a generating resource would

   18          include at least all fixed costs, fuel costs, non-fuel variable costs, market revenues, and

   19          other direct costs and revenues.




                                                         13
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 39 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/18/2026 - PAGE 14 OF 30

                                                                                      PUD 2026-000046
                                                                  Responsive Testimony of Frank J. Beling

    1    Q.    IS IT IMPORTANT TO INCLUDE CONTRACTED RESOURCES IN THE FAIL-

    2          SAFE ANALYSIS CALCULATION OF THE SANCG?

    3    A.    Yes. It is important to include all resource ownership structures in the calculation of the

    4          SANCG because they will all affect the cost impact to the system, and therefore, to other

    5          customer classes.

    6    Q.    WHY SHOULD THE FAIL-SAFE ANALYSIS CALCULATION OF THE SANCG

    7          CONSIDER ALL NEW GENERATION RESOURCES ADDED AFTER JULY 1,

    8          2026, INSTEAD OF ONLY INCLUDING THE “INCREMENTAL RESOURCES”

    9          ADDED TO SERVE NEW LARGE LOADS?

   10    A.    Resource planning for electric utilities is complex, and although new large loads are a

   11          significant driver for the addition of new generation resources, there are also other drivers

   12          that affect the need for resources such as:

   13              •   Load growth of existing customer loads (non-large loads);

   14              •   Retirement of existing generation resources;

   15              •   Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”) rule changes that affect the required level of

   16                  planning reserve margin; and

   17              •   Changes in accreditation for existing generation resources.

   18          Utility resource planning must plan for an uncertain future given all of the factors listed

   19          above. In addition, often the commercial operation date (“COD”) of generation does not

   20          exactly coincide with the start date of a new load. Because the need for a new generation

   21          resource may be driven by any combination of the factors listed above, and because it may

   22          not align with a specific new load coming online, it is very difficult to specifically identify

   23          which resource(s) should be considered to be the “incremental resource” to serve new large



                                                         14
 CASE PUD 2026-000046 ENTRY NO. 39 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 09/18/2026 - PAGE 15 OF 30

                                                                                     PUD 2026-000046
                                                                 Responsive Testimony of Frank J. Beling

    1          loads. Instead, I recommend considering all new generation resources (added after July 1,

    2          2026) as being part of the portfolio that is serving any new large loads.

    3    Q.    WHY IS IT IMPORTANT TO CONSIDER THE TOTAL NET REVENUE

    4          REQUIREMENT OF A GENERATION RESOURCE IN THE FAIL-SAFE

    5          ANALYSIS CALCULATION OF THE SANCG?

    6    A.    Different generation resources create value in different ways. Some generation resources

    7          produce high levels of energy value in the SPP market, while other types of resources

    8          provide mostly capacity value. Because the Company’s resource portfolio includes a range

    9          of varying resource types, it is important to include all the costs and value that different

   10          generation resources create. If certain components were excluded, such as fuel cost or

   11          market revenue, the calculation would be skewed and would unfairly favor or penalize

   12          certain types of resources or ownership structures.

   13    Q.    WHY IS IT IMPORTANT TO ESTABLISH DEFINED PARAMETERS AND

   14          METHODOLOGY FOR THE FAIL-SAFE ANALYSIS?

   15    A.    It is important to establish defined parameters and a clear methodology for the fail-safe

   16          analysis to ensure that it is an effective tool to measure impact on other Company

   17          customers. If certain cost components or generation resources are not considered in the

   18          fail-safe analysis, the result will not represent the true impact of serving new large load

   19          customers.

    1                                  VI.      XLPL Price Determination

    2    Q.     PLEASE DESCRIBE HOW THE COMPANY WILL ALLOCATE COSTS TO THE

    3           XLPL CLASS.

    4    A.     The Company indicated it will use the Maximum Contract Demands for each load when

    5           determining the revenue requirement allocation to the XLPL class. 13

    6    Q.     DOES       USING       THE       MAXIMUM          CONTRACT           DEMANDS          WHEN

    7           DETERMINING CLASS COST ALLOCATION PROVIDE ANY PROTECTIONS

    8           TO OTHER CUSTOMER CLASSES?

    9    A.     Yes. In the case where an XLPL customer has contracted for a certain level but then later

   10           reduces its actual level of load, using the Maximum Contract Demands maintains an

   11           alignment between the costs assigned to the XLPL class and the generation that the

   12           Company would have had to procure to serve the customer. This would help prevent cost

   13           shifts to other classes when an XLPL customer reduces its load while still under contract

   14           with the Company.

   15    Q.     PLEASE DESCRIBE HOW THE COMPANY WILL DEVELOP THE TARIFF

   16           CHARGES FOR THE XLPL CLASS.

   17    A.     The Company indicated it will use the minimum billing values for each load when

   18           determining the prices charged to customers under the XLPL class. 14 In other words, once

   19           costs have been allocated to the XLPL class through a COSS calculation, the specific rates




         13
            Direct Test. of Matthew DeCourcey for Okla. Gas and Elec. Co. 20:15–19 (June 17, 2026) [hereinafter

    1              and charges will be determined by dividing the allocated costs by the class billing units,

    2              and the class billing units will be determined using the minimum billing values.

    3    Q.        PLEASE DESCRIBE HOW THE COMPANY WILL BILL CUSTOMERS IN THE

    4              XLPL CLASS.

    5    A.        The Company indicated it will bill XLPL customers using the greater of the actual usage

    6              or the minimum billing values, and that this methodology would apply both to demand-

    7              based charges 15 and to energy-based charges.16

    8    Q.        PLEASE IDENTIFY ANY DISCREPANCIES BETWEEN HOW THE COMPANY

    9              WOULD DEVELOP CHARGES AND HOW THE COMPANY WOULD BILL

   10              CUSTOMERS.

   11    A.        As I described, the Company will set rates using the billing minimums but will bill

   12              customers at the greater of the billing minimums or the actual usage. In many cases, the

   18          analysis. I supported the use of a properly designed analysis to identify and mitigate any
